mcp_servers.name: claude.ai Scholarly Full Text Article Access with LibKey

commands.name: figma:figma-code-connect
commands.description: (figma) Creates and maintains Figma Code Connect template files that map Figma components to code snippets. Use when the user mentions Code Connect, Figma component mapping, design-to-code translation, or asks to create/update .figma.ts or .figma.js files.

commands.name: figma:figma-code-workflows
commands.description: (figma) Import or upload local HTML or project files into Figma, choose editable Design frames, runnable Code Layers or standalone Code (also known as Make), and repair imported previews. Use only when the user explicitly names editable Design layers, a runnable Code Layer, or a standalone Code/Make file, or supplies a Figma file key/link as the import destination. Generic code or code-component requests need output clarification before using this workflow.

commands.name: figma:figma-create-new-file
commands.description: (figma) Always use this skill when the user wants to create a new Figma Design, FigJam, or Slides file. You MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call.

commands.name: figma:figma-design-to-code
commands.description: (figma) **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE calling the `get_design_context` Figma MCP tool. You MUST trigger this skill whenever the user wants to implement, build, port, or code up a Figma design as code. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.

commands.name: figma:figma-generate-design
commands.description: (figma) Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, form, dashboard, list, table, card, header, message preview, or other composed product UI in Figma from code or a description—even when the user calls that composed UI a component. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.

commands.name: figma:figma-generate-diagram
commands.description: (figma) MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).

commands.name: figma:figma-generate-library
commands.description: (figma) Build or update a professional-grade design system in Figma from a codebase. Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.

commands.name: figma:figma-generative-plugins
commands.description: (figma) **MANDATORY prerequisite** — load this skill before calling `create_generative_plugin` or `update_generative_plugin`. Use when the user asks to create, author, change, fix, or extend a reusable generative Figma plugin.

commands.name: figma:figma-implement-motion
commands.description: (figma) Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.

commands.name: figma:figma-shaders
commands.description: (figma) **MANDATORY prerequisite** — load this skill before calling `create_shader` or `update_shader`. Use when the user asks to create, author, change, fix, or iterate on a shader effect, shader fill, custom effect, custom fill, or procedural shader in Figma.

commands.name: figma:figma-spec
commands.description: (figma) This skill is required to create, read, edit, review, or comment on Figma specs. You must read it when working on a PRD, brief, RFC or any kind of document in either a standalone Figma spec or a Figma spec embedded in a Figma Design or Figjam file.

commands.name: figma:figma-swiftui
commands.description: (figma) SwiftUI ↔ Figma translation. Use whenever the user mentions Swift, SwiftUI, iOS, iPhone, or iPad — in EITHER direction — translating a Figma design into SwiftUI (design → code), or pushing SwiftUI views / screens / tokens back into a Figma file (code → design). Triggers on phrases like 'implement this Figma design in SwiftUI', 'build this screen in Swift', 'push this SwiftUI view to Figma', 'mirror my Swift code in a Figma file', or whenever a Figma URL appears alongside `.swift` files / an `.xcodeproj`. Routes to a direction-specific reference doc; loads alongside `figma-use` for the code → design path.

commands.name: figma:figma-use
commands.description: (figma) **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `use_figma` tool call. NEVER call `use_figma` directly without loading this skill first. Skipping it causes common, hard-to-debug failures. Trigger whenever the user wants to perform a write action or a unique read action that requires JavaScript execution in the Figma file context — e.g. create/edit/delete nodes, set up variables or tokens, build components and variants, modify auto-layout or fills, bind variables to properties, or inspect file structure programmatically.

commands.name: figma:figma-use-figjam
commands.description: (figma) This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the FigJam context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.

commands.name: figma:figma-use-motion
commands.description: (figma) Motion / animation context for the `use_figma` MCP tool — animating Figma nodes via manual keyframes, animation styles, easing, and timeline duration. Load alongside figma-use whenever a task involves adding, editing, or inspecting animation on a node. Also covers working with custom animation styles.

commands.name: figma:figma-use-slides
commands.description: (figma) This skill helps agents use Figma's use_figma MCP tool in the Slides context. Can be used alongside figma-use which has foundational context for using the use_figma tool.

commands.name: design
commands.description: Grant or revoke Claude agent access to your Design projects

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: import-memory
commands.description: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: morning
commands.description: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: skill-creator
commands.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: schedule
commands.description: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule.

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

commands.name: run
commands.description: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

commands.name: run-skill-generator
commands.description: Author or improve the run-<unit> skill - a per-project skill that tells agents how to build, launch, and drive this project's app. Use when the user asks to set up the project, get it running, write run instructions, or verify build/run steps work from a clean environment.

commands.name: plugin-authoring
commands.description: Make a mod: a change to Claude's own interface or behaviour, such as a panel or pane that stays beside the chat and updates, a band, status line, toast, slash command, or hook on tool calls. Use to make, change or debug a mod or its hooks module.

commands.description: Teach auto mode about your environment, plus optional rule tweaks

commands.name: design

commands.name: design-sync
commands.description: Push a React design system to claude.ai/design. This runs a converter that bundles the real component code (from Storybook or a bare package) and uploads it. Use when the user runs /design-sync or says "sync my design system to Claude Design".

commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.name: code-review
commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's recipe covers them) at the effort level given first, before any target (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings to many, some uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply them to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default.

commands.name: simplify
commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.name: batch
commands.description: Research and plan a large-scale change, then execute it in parallel across 5–30 isolated worktree agents that each open a PR.

commands.name: fewer-permission-prompts
commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

commands.name: doctor
commands.description: Health-check the user's Claude Code setup and fix issues: diagnose installation health — what the `claude doctor` terminal diagnostics cover — from local data (duplicate or leftover installs, PATH, unparseable settings files, broken or colliding agent definitions, skills whose frontmatter fails to parse); find unused skills, MCP servers, and plugins versus their context cost and disable dead weight; deduplicate local CLAUDE.md files against checked-in ones; trim checked-in CLAUDE.md files by cutting content a session could derive from the codebase (directory layouts, tech-stack lists, architecture overviews) while keeping gotchas, rationale, and non-standard conventions; migrate always-loaded CLAUDE.md guidance into lazy skills and nested CLAUDE.md files; flag slow hooks and context-heavy extensions; check the installed version is current; make auto mode the default permission mode; and pre-approve frequently denied read-only commands. Use when the user asks for a doctor run, checkup, audit, tune-up, or cleanup of their Claude Code setup or configuration.

commands.name: loop
commands.description: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace.

commands.name: schedule

commands.name: claude-api
commands.description:
Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

commands.name: run

commands.name: docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of Microsoft Word Documents, such as 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', 'microsoft doc'. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead, even if they will email or print it. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: google-workspace
commands.description: Read this before the first Google Drive, Docs, Sheets or Slides connector call whenever the task creates or changes a Google file. Use this skill whenever the user wants to create or change a Google Doc, Sheet or Slides file in their Google Drive. Triggers include: a request that names Google Docs, Sheets, Slides or Drive and asks to make, edit, format, copy or rename a file; a docs.google.com link with a request to change that file, even a one-line fix or suggested edits; and any follow-up change to a Google file from earlier in the chat, even "change it" or "add a tab". Includes helper scripts for document positions, cell ranges and slide layout. However, if the user asks for a doc, deck or spreadsheet without naming Google, or gives a Google file only as source material for something new, use Claude's own output type instead. Do NOT use for read-only questions about a Google file, or for Word, Excel, PowerPoint or PDF files. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: import-memory
commands.description: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: morning
commands.description: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: skill-creator
commands.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

536	The quad **without** `source_color`. Godot’s 3D rendering pipeline operates in Linear color space. When a texture is imported or sampled with `source_color`, Godot assumes it was authored in sRGB (how monitors display color) and automatically applies an inverse gamma correction curve (~power of 2.2) to convert it to Linear space, mathematically altering the raw pixel values. Sampling without `source_color` reads the exact raw data bytes from the file.

The game in its mechanics has multiple sneek requirements, to avoid detections from the NPCs. 


- Why the player needs to see it:
The vision cone is indicator as well it serves as the perception of what the NPC is able to detect the presence of the raccoon in his surrounding. The game has a lots of tasks that are expected to be done while sneaking around and avoid detection, so it's important that the players understand what the spotting vision is limited to or the detection feedback is working to play the game.

- What the cone does:
  - The state: The detection system will follows the color pattern of being tinge of yellow for indicating the general sight of vision, which will also increase and reduce depending upon the raccoon's/player's movements, and when detected we go a alerted state for the NPC and the raccoon.
  - The two colours: The pale yellow and red are the two main vision colors.
  - The change: When spotted the color should snap to red for a 2 seconds indicating the actions to the player along with state of alerted. If the player wants to fade the status away he needs to run away from the vicinity of the alerted NPC or hide away to become undetected again.

  (My answers to Claude Code's questions, 26 Oct 2026, in my own words. Claude Code fixed the spelling and typos and added full stops and commas. This "why" replaces my first answer, which was about the moods in general.)

- What the cone does, round 2 (26 Oct 2026):
  - How long it stays red: 2 seconds. (I first wrote "Vanishing after 3 frames so the player understands he has been spotted"; Claude Code pointed out that 3 frames is 0.1 s at 30 fps and 0.02 s at 144 fps, and I picked 2 seconds from its options.)
  - What starts the red: the moment he's spotted. (Picked from Claude Code's options.)
  - Back to yellow: There should be no fade to yellow.
  - After the red: Completely fade all the vision cones, make the NPC confused with the "??" around his head looking around and then walk back, and after like 5 seconds bring the vision cone back.
  - When the confused part happens: This confused action happens after he has shooed him away and after the raccoon has evaded the sight.
  - When the cones start: no cones until he reaches the camp. Yes, let's show him the tasks as some sort of tutorial workflow prompting him to open Tab. Before this there should be no tasks other than "identify the music", and then the "rock the party" main task should have sub tasks like steal marshmallows and all others which we have. It's a interactive tutorial style.

  (My answers, in my own words, with spelling fixed by Claude Code.)

- The gaps, filled by Claude Code because I asked it to ("take liberties with the gaps that feel approriate", 26 Oct 2026). These are Claude Code's choices, not mine:
  - The fade-out: when the 2 s of red are up, all the cones fade out together over 0.5 s. During the 2 s only the cone of the camper who spotted him is red; the others stay yellow until they fade with it.
  - Coming back: 5 s after a camper starts walking back from the confused looking-around, that camper's cone fades back in, yellow, over 0.5 s.
  - The length: while the cones show after a spotting, each stays as long as it was while its camper watched (7 m standing, shorter while he sneaks), not the 14 m an alarmed camper sees.
  - The names: "identify the music" is the task already in the game, "Investigate the music". The main task is "Rock the party", with the camp's tasks as its sub-tasks.
  - The tutorial: he reaches the camp and "Investigate the music" is ticked off. The game pauses and a note says to press Tab. THE PLAN opens, showing "Rock the party" and its sub-tasks, and the note tells him to sneak so they don't see him. He closes it with Tab, the game carries on, and the cones fade in.
  - The split: when the cones show, the campers' "??" search and the timers are the game's behaviour, written by Claude Code in GDScript. The yellow, the 2 s of red and the fades are my shader's job, driven from that behaviour.

- The script and variable that hold it:

- The other moods in the game, and why I picked this one:


### The effect
- Shader file: `shaders/vision_cone.gdshader` (picked from Claude Code's options, 27 Oct 2026)
- shader_type and render_mode (my words, 28 Oct 2026):
  - `shader_type spatial;`: In Godot, 3D materials require the spatial shader type to interact with the 3D rendering pipeline.
  - `render_mode blend_mix, unshaded, depth_draw_opaque;`: `blend_mix` enables standard alpha transparency, `unshaded` prevents the environment's lights and shadows from altering the cone's flat colors, and `depth_draw_opaque` ensures the transparent cone correctly depth-sorts against other transparent elements.
- The object it colours, and how that object is drawn: each camper's vision cone, a fan of 24 triangles on the ground under their eyes, built in code (`scripts/vision_cone.gd`, `_build_cone`). Its corners carry vertex colours, white, with alpha 0.55 at the camper fading to 0.12 at the far edge. Until my shader is in, it's drawn with a StandardMaterial3D made in code: unshaded, see-through, vertex colours as its colour, both sides drawn, no fog. (These facts are from the code, written in by Claude Code.)

| Uniform | Type | Hint | Default | Set by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `alarm` | float | `hint_range(0.0, 1.0)` | 0.0 | The game, every frame: 0 = the yellow, 1 = the red |
| `shown` | float | `hint_range(0.0, 1.0)` | 1.0 | The game, every frame: 0 = gone, 1 = fully shown (the fades) |
| `watch_color` | vec4: a colour and its see-through amount | `source_color` | the game's yellow, `WATCHING`: (1.0, 0.93, 0.62, 0.5) | Its default, which a material can change in the Inspector |
| `alarm_color` | vec4: a colour and its see-through amount | `source_color` | the game's red, `SEEING`: (1.0, 0.33, 0.27, 0.65) | Its default, which a material can change in the Inspector |

(Picked from Claude Code's options on 26 and 27 Oct 2026: the names, what 0 and 1 mean for `alarm` and `shown`, their defaults, the hints, and the two colours as knobs keeping the game's colours and see-through amounts.)

### The colour line
(the one line inside fragment() that changes the colour)

My choices for it (picked from Claude Code's options, 27 Oct 2026):
- As `alarm` goes from 0 to 1, the colour blends smoothly from `watch_color` to `alarm_color`, halfway at 0.5.
- How see-through the cone is at a pixel: its tip-to-edge fade × the colour's own amount × `shown`.

### Rules
- The uniform's value when the mood starts, and when it ends:
  `alarm` jumps from 0 to 1 the moment he's spotted, and stays at 1 through the 2 s of red and the fade-out after it. It's back at 0 when the cone comes back. `shown` is 1 while the cone shows; it goes to 0 after the red, and back to 1 when the cone comes back.
- How long the change takes (seconds, give or take one frame), the same at 30, 60 and 144 fps:
  `alarm` takes no time: it snaps. `shown` goes from 1 to 0 over 0.5 s, starting 2 s after the spotting, and from 0 to 1 over 0.5 s when the cone comes back, 5 s after its camper starts walking back. Each takes the same time at 30, 60 and 144 fps, give or take one frame.

  (These two are from my design above, as Claude Code put it together; I confirmed it on 27 Oct 2026.)
- If the mood starts again mid-change: restart, extend or ignore?
  Restart: the red lasts 2 s from the latest spotting, whether another camper spots him or the same one sees him again.
- Scaled or unscaled time under Engine.time_scale, and what it does while paused:
  Unscaled: always 2 real seconds, whatever speed the game runs at. While the game is paused, the red and the fades freeze where they are and carry on afterwards.
- The value if the mood ends before the change finishes:
  The red still runs its full 2 s and then fades, even if he's already hidden.

  (The three answers above are mine, picked from Claude Code's options on 26 Oct 2026.)
- With several copies of the object, how each gets its own value:
  One material per cone: each cone makes its own ShaderMaterial from my one shader, and the game sets each one's values. (Picked from Claude Code's options on 27 Oct 2026.)

### Boundaries
(what this change must not touch)

When my shader and its driver go in, these stay exactly as they are (ticked by me from Claude Code's list, 27 Oct 2026):
- how he moves and collides, and which keys do what;
- the campers' behaviour (when they see him, guard, chase, shoo and search) and all its timings, as built on 26 Oct;
- everything else's look: only the cones change, and the trees, the fire, the icons and the other shaders stay the same;
- no earlier test's expectations change (added at my request on 27 Oct 2026, after Claude Code pointed out that the assignment lists it).

### Evidence split
| Rule | Checked by (test or my eyes) | How |
|---|---|---|
| Spotted: `alarm` snaps to 1 and the red lasts 2 s; it starts over when he's re-spotted, and still runs its 2 s if he's lost early | A headless test | Claude's driver test reads `alarm` every frame at 30, 60 and 144 fps while he's spotted in play at the camp, and measures the times |
| The fades: `shown` 1 to 0 over 0.5 s after the red, 0 to 1 over 0.5 s when the cone comes back | A headless test | The same test measures them on the game's clock |
| Paused: the red and the fades freeze. Slowed down: always 2 real seconds | A headless test | The test pauses the game and sets `Engine.time_scale`, then checks `alarm` and `shown` |
| Each cone has its own value: only the spotter's goes red | Both | The test checks each cone's `alarm` and `shown`; I check in play that only one cone turns red |

(Picked by me from Claude Code's options, 27 Oct 2026. "Lost early" is in the first row because I chose a test for every timing rule.)

### Predicted pixels
| Pixel | Its colour now | At 0.0 (Yellow: 255, 237, 158) | At 0.5 (Blend: 255, 160, 113) | At 1.0 (Red: 255, 84, 69) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Base at Camper** (Vertex Alpha 0.55 over Grass 80, 120, 80) | 80, 120, 80 | 176, 184, 123 | 176, 142, 98 | 176, 100, 74 |
| **Far Edge** (Vertex Alpha 0.12 over Grass 80, 120, 80) | 80, 120, 80 | 100, 133, 89 | 100, 124, 83 | 100, 115, 78 |

### Hint experiment predictions
| Grey in the file | Quad with source_color | Quad without |
|---|---|---|
| 64 (0.25) | ~0.05 (Darkened via sRGB curve) | 0.25 |
| 128 (0.50) | ~0.21 (Darkened via sRGB curve) | 0.50 |
| 192 (0.75) | ~0.53 (Darkened via sRGB curve) | 0.75 |

**Which quad shows the file's values unchanged, and why:**
The quad **without** `source_color`. Godot’s 3D rendering pipeline operates in Linear color space. When a texture is imported or sampled with `source_color`, Godot assumes it was authored in sRGB (how monitors display color) and automatically applies an inverse gamma correction curve (~power of 2.2) to convert it to Linear space, mathematically altering the raw pixel values. Sampling without `source_color` reads the exact raw data bytes from the file.

### Material plan (the textured shader)
**The object, and the lighting I'll judge it under:** The 24-triangle vision cone fan on the ground, viewed under the game's flat-shaded, unlit night environment where only ALBEDO and ALPHA determine the final pixel output.

| Texture | Role | Source | What its numbers mean | Colour or data | compress/mode | compress/normal_map | mipmaps/generate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cone_edge_mask.png` | Softens the harsh side edges of the geometric triangles to look more like a projected light | 2D image | 1.0 (white) in the center fading to 0.0 (black) at the left and right borders | Data | Lossless / VRAM uncompressed | False | False (prevents edge bleeding at distances) |

| Uniform | Type | Hint | Range | Default | Group | What changes on screen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `edge_softness` | float | `hint_range` | 0.0 to 1.0 | 0.1 | Edge Mask | How wide the blurred transition is at the side borders of the cone |
| `mask_texture` | sampler2D | `filter_linear` | N/A | empty | Edge Mask | Applies the horizontal gradient falloff to the cone |

**How the two materials differ, and why:**
The untextured version relies solely on the CPU-generated vertex colors (alpha 0.55 to 0.12) to fade the cone outward, leaving sharp geometric edges on the sides. The textured material multiplies this vertex alpha by the `mask_texture`, resulting in a cone that smoothly fades out both over distance (via vertices) and at its peripheral vision edges (via the texture).

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/run-test.sh <test-file.gd | --flag-test> <fps>
# The course's Assignment 5 wrapper, adapted for this repository by Claude Code:
# - the Godot project is the repository root, so --path . (the course's has --path godot);
# - Godot isn't on the PATH on the author's machine, so it is found from GODOT, then `godot`,
#   then the two places the .bat launchers look;
# - the earlier checks run inside the main scene from a flag (`-- --sound-test`), so an
#   argument that starts with -- runs main.tscn with that flag instead of a tests/ script.
# Exit status 124 means the test hung.
set -o pipefail
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1
godot="${GODOT:-$(command -v godot || true)}"
for g in ../Godot/Godot_v4.7.2-stable_win64_console.exe "$LOCALAPPDATA/Programs/Godot/Godot_v4.7.2-stable_win64_console.exe"; do
	if [ -z "$godot" ] && [ -f "$g" ]; then godot="$g"; fi
done
if [ -z "$godot" ]; then echo "Godot not found: set GODOT to its executable"; exit 1; fi
mkdir -p logs
if [[ "$1" == --* ]]; then
	log="logs/${1#--}_${2}fps.log"
	timeout 120 "$godot" --headless --path . --fixed-fps "$2" -- "$1" 2>&1 | tee "$log"
else
	log="logs/$(basename "$1" .gd)_${2}fps.log"
	timeout 120 "$godot" --headless --path . --script "res://tests/$1" --fixed-fps "$2" 2>&1 | tee "$log"
fi
status=$?
if grep -qE "SHADER ERROR|SCRIPT ERROR" "$log"; then status=1; fi
exit $status

1	# The Noise Next Door
2	
3	A raccoon just wants a quiet night in his tree. Then a party starts right underneath it.
4	
5	He sneaks down to prank the partiers, gets chased into town wearing a camper's red beanie, becomes the neighbourhood's masked bandit, and is finally driven home by that same camper, just in time for the next party. It's slapstick with no dialogue: the story is told through what the player does and how people react.
6	
7	Made for CSYE 7270 (Fall 2026): one game, built up one assignment at a time.
8	
9	| Assignment | What it added | Submitted as |
10	|---|---|---|
11	| [Assignment 5: Shaders, Materials, and the Godot Shading Language](#assignment-5-shaders-and-materials-in-progress) | In progress: hand-written shaders and materials, for the campers' vision cones and a textured 3D object | branch `assignment-5`, not tagged yet |
12	| [Assignment 3: Your First 3D Game Assets with Claude, the Blender MCP, and Blender](#assignment-3-the-three-blender-assets) | Three props built in Blender through the Blender MCP, a Godot asset room and a headless check | tag `a3` |
13	| [Assignment 2: Generate Art, Sound, and Music for Your Game](#assignment-2-the-asset-slice) | The asset slice: the forest clearing with the generated poses, sounds and music | tag `a2` |
14	
15	After Assignment 3, the game also got its title screen, the night, the humans, level 1's camp, THE PLAN and the party's sound waves. [Run it](#run-it) covers them.
16	
17	![The storyboard](design/storyboard/storyboard-sheet.svg)
18	
19	## Run it
20	
21	You need Godot 4.7.2. The project uses the Forward+ renderer.
22	
23	- **Windows:** double-click `Play The Noise Next Door.bat`, or `Edit in Godot.bat` to open the editor. They look for Godot in the `GODOT` environment variable, then in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Godot`, then in your Downloads folder. The first run takes a few seconds longer while Godot imports the raccoon model.
24	- **Anywhere:** run `godot --path .` from this folder. On a fresh clone, first run `godot --headless --path . --import` once (or open the project in the editor), so the raccoon model is imported.
25	
26	**The title screen:** Up and Down (or W and S, or the mouse) pick a line, and Enter, Space, E or a click chooses it. Continue stays faint until there are save states to continue from. Settings has the music and effects volumes (Left and Right) and full screen, and Esc goes back. The title is the game's own world at night, seen from where your title picture was taken, so New Game changes nothing but the camera: it glides in to the close-up of the raccoon asleep in his hollow, the lullaby playing on, and W, A, S or D wakes him to start. Any `--` argument other than the title's own skips the title, so the checks below still work as before.
27	
28	**Level 1's campsite** (23 Oct 2026, `scripts/campsite.gd`): the party is set up about 20 seconds' walk east of his tree, at the end of a trodden trail along the edge of the trees: a fire pit, two tents, logs, the cooler, a table with the laptop, pizza and a donut, a speaker and string lights. The camper is pegging out his tent with a mallet, and the low-poly man and the simple girl dance by the fire on the music's beat. The speaker plays a party beat; since 25 Oct 2026 you don't hear it, you see it, as its sound waves (below). The people react to him: seen (sneak to get closer), all three take fright; the girl hides behind the low-poly man and cowers, the men stand guard, and if he hangs about they chase him off, shooing him away when they catch him. Pictures are in [design/level1/campsite/](design/level1/campsite/).
29	
30	**Level 1's tasks** (24 Oct 2026, `scripts/camp_puzzles.gd`): the to-do list is now the camp's three tasks; the bin, lid, cans and gnome by his tree are still there to play with, and he still naps in his hollow, but they aren't tasks any more. The people keep to looping routines, which tell you when each one is busy: the camper pegs out his tent, then sits roasting marshmallows by the fire with his back to his backpack, then goes to the table for pizza; the low-poly man dances, then fetches a drink from the cooler; the girl dances, then warms her hands at the fire. Next to something he can use, a chalk E shows; hold E for slow jobs, and a ring fills as he works. Jobs make noise, and the people hear it and come to look ("?" over their heads), but the music drowns a lot of it out, and while they dance they're lost in the music and see less. The tasks:
31	- **Steal the marshmallows:** while the camper roasts with his back to it, hold E at his backpack to unzip it; the bag tumbles out. Carry it home to his stash under his tree. Running with it, it crinkles.
32	- **Turn the music off:** hold E at the plug under the table to tug it out with his teeth. The music stops, which ticks it off, and the dancers stop dead for two seconds: get away then. Then everyone wonders where the music went, and the low-poly man finds the plug wherever he left it and plugs it back in. Without the music, every noise carries further.
33	- **Raid the cooler:** hold E to nose its lid open (a clunk the camper hears if he's by the fire), or wait for the low-poly man, who sometimes leaves it open after his drink. Take the sausages home.
34	- **Caught carrying their things,** a man snatches them back and the puzzle resets: the bag zipped back in, the sausages back in the shut cooler.
35	
36	There's no ending yet. Pictures are in [design/level1/tasks/](design/level1/tasks/).
37	
38	**The tutorial at the camp and the campers' cones** (26 Oct 2026, `scripts/camp_tutorial.gd`, `scripts/camp_person.gd`, `scripts/vision_cone.gd`): on the way there, the only task is to investigate the music. When he reaches the camp, the game pauses and a note at the bottom says to press Tab. THE PLAN opens with the camp's three tasks on it, under one main task, Rock the party, and the note says to sneak past them; Tab again, and the game carries on. Only then can the campers see him, and their cones show on the ground: pale yellow while they watch, shorter while he sneaks. The moment one spots him, that one's cone turns red for 2 seconds, and then all the cones go while they guard, chase and shoo as before. Once he's got away, they look about, confused, with "??" over their heads, then walk back; each one's cone comes back 5 seconds after they start back. The fades on the cones are still to come, with the cone shader for Assignment 5.
39	
40	**The party next door** (25 Oct 2026, `scripts/sound_waves.gd`): under the title the night is quiet; New Game starts the party up. You don't hear it (his lullaby plays on); you see it, as its sound waves. They are drawn like the thought icons, three hand-scribbled wavy white lines. On the beat, while the speaker's off the screen, a set pulses on the edge of the screen the music's coming from, so you can always tell which way to go; once the speaker's on the screen, the sets come out of the speaker itself. Asleep in his hollow, he sleeps on through it, untroubled. Pictures are in [design/level1/waves/](design/level1/waves/).
41	
42	**Controls:** WASD or the arrow keys to move, Shift to run, Ctrl or C to sneak, F to jump (tap it for a small hop, hold it for a full jump), E or a click to grab or drop, Space to chitter, and the mouse wheel to zoom. Walk into a tree to climb it. Then W and S climb up and down, A and D go round the trunk, and E or F lets go. Climb to the top of the home pine to get into the hollow. Esc pauses. M turns the music on and off, and N does the same for the sound effects. Tab brings up THE PLAN, the level's tasks on a torn notebook page, crossed off as they're done (the camp's tasks appear on it with the tutorial at the camp); the task to follow now waits at the bottom of the screen, and a task just done comes up there crossed off. V opens a panel for trying out camera views live; its "Copy numbers" button copies the settings.
43	
44	**The automated sound check:** run `godot --headless --path . -- --sound-test`. It plays a scripted input sequence, counts how often each sound effect starts, and checks the music's pause, mute, loop and end behaviour. It prints a table, and its exit code is 0 only if every check passes (`scripts/sound_test.gd`).
45	
46	**The campsite check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --camp-test`. It puts the raccoon near the camp sneaking, in plain sight, lingering, up a tree, gone and chittering out of sight, and checks how each of the three takes it (`scripts/camp_test.gd`). Add `--camp-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.
47	
48	**The tasks check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --tasks-test`. It walks the three through their routines, then plays each task with E as you would: the marshmallows caught and snatched back, then stolen cleanly and taken home; the music off, the dancers frozen, and the plug found and put back; a noise drowned by the music but heard without it; and the cooler raided. It checks the to-do list ticks each one off (`scripts/tasks_test.gd`). Add `--tasks-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.
49	
50	**The sound waves check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --waves-test`. It checks a set of waves goes out on the party's beat and fades after its time; that by his tree and along the trail they're on the edge of the screen the music comes from, and at the camp they come out of the speaker; and that with the music stopped no more come (`scripts/waves_test.gd`). Add `--waves-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.
51	
52	**THE PLAN check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --plan-test`. It brings the plan up with Tab and puts it away, checks V has the camera panel, then ticks tasks off and checks what comes up at the bottom of the screen: a task just done, crossed off, and gone again; the key task waiting there until he reaches the camp; and the page crossing off what's been done (`scripts/plan_test.gd`). Add `--plan-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.
53	
54	**The tutorial and cones check:** run `godot --headless --path . -- --cones-test`. It puts the raccoon in plain sight at the camp and checks that nobody sees him before the tutorial; that the tutorial pauses the game, ignores Esc, shows Rock the party and its tasks on Tab and carries on after a second Tab; that the spotter's cone is red, every cone shows through the red, and every cone goes 2.5 s after the spotting; that after the chase each of them is confused for 3 s and their cone comes back 5 s after they start back; and that Rock the party is ticked off with its last task (`scripts/cones_test.gd`). 56	**The title screen check:** run `godot --headless --path . -- --title-test`. It moves through the menu with the keys and the mouse, changes the volumes and checks they reach the buses and the settings file, checks the menu's keys leave him asleep, then chooses New Game and checks the way in: the same scene throughout with nothing laid over it, the camera ending in the nap close-up, the lullaby carrying on, the party next door quiet under the title and starting with New Game, silent, with the lullaby playing on and his nap going on untroubled by it, that first nap not counting as one of his naps, and a move key waking him and bringing in the forest music and the key task at the bottom of the screen. It puts your settings file back afterwards (`scripts/title_test.gd`). Run in a window with `--title-shots=<folder>` as well, it saves pictures of the way in. `godot --path . -- --title-shot=out.png` saves a picture of the title screen.

To remake the character-sheet images and the raccoon's cut-outs, run `godot --path . --script res://design/character/make_character_sheet.gd`, then copy the five cut-outs the slice uses into `assets/characters/raccoon/`. # The Noise Next Door

A raccoon just wants a quiet night in his tree. Then a party starts right underneath it.

He sneaks down to prank the partiers, gets chased into town wearing a camper's red beanie, becomes the neighbourhood's masked bandit, and is finally driven home by that same camper, just in time for the next party. It's slapstick with no dialogue: the story is told through what the player does and how people react.

Made for CSYE 7270 (Fall 2026): one game, built up one assignment at a time.

| Assignment | What it added | Submitted as |
|---|---|---|
| [Assignment 5: Shaders, Materials, and the Godot Shading Language](#assignment-5-shaders-and-materials-in-progress) | In progress: hand-written shaders and materials, for the campers' vision cones and a textured 3D object | branch `assignment-5`, not tagged yet |
| [Assignment 3: Your First 3D Game Assets with Claude, the Blender MCP, and Blender](#assignment-3-the-three-blender-assets) | Three props built in Blender through the Blender MCP, a Godot asset room and a headless check | tag `a3` |
| [Assignment 2: Generate Art, Sound, and Music for Your Game](#assignment-2-the-asset-slice) | The asset slice: the forest clearing with the generated poses, sounds and music | tag `a2` |

After Assignment 3, the game also got its title screen, the night, the humans, level 1's camp, THE PLAN and the party's sound waves. [Run it](#run-it) covers them.

![The storyboard](design/storyboard/storyboard-sheet.svg)

## Run it

You need Godot 4.7.2. The project uses the Forward+ renderer.

- **Windows:** double-click `Play The Noise Next Door.bat`, or `Edit in Godot.bat` to open the editor. They look for Godot in the `GODOT` environment variable, then in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Godot`, then in your Downloads folder. The first run takes a few seconds longer while Godot imports the raccoon model.
- **Anywhere:** run `godot --path .` from this folder. On a fresh clone, first run `godot --headless --path . --import` once (or open the project in the editor), so the raccoon model is imported.

**The title screen:** Up and Down (or W and S, or the mouse) pick a line, and Enter, Space, E or a click chooses it. Continue stays faint until there are save states to continue from. Settings has the music and effects volumes (Left and Right) and full screen, and Esc goes back. The title is the game's own world at night, seen from where your title picture was taken, so New Game changes nothing but the camera: it glides in to the close-up of the raccoon asleep in his hollow, the lullaby playing on, and W, A, S or D wakes him to start. Any `--` argument other than the title's own skips the title, so the checks below still work as before.

**Level 1's campsite** (23 Oct 2026, `scripts/campsite.gd`): the party is set up about 20 seconds' walk east of his tree, at the end of a trodden trail along the edge of the trees: a fire pit, two tents, logs, the cooler, a table with the laptop, pizza and a donut, a speaker and string lights. The camper is pegging out his tent with a mallet, and the low-poly man and the simple girl dance by the fire on the music's beat. The speaker plays a party beat; since 25 Oct 2026 you don't hear it, you see it, as its sound waves (below). The people react to him: seen (sneak to get closer), all three take fright; the girl hides behind the low-poly man and cowers, the men stand guard, and if he hangs about they chase him off, shooing him away when they catch him. Pictures are in [design/level1/campsite/](design/level1/campsite/).

**Level 1's tasks** (24 Oct 2026, `scripts/camp_puzzles.gd`): the to-do list is now the camp's three tasks; the bin, lid, cans and gnome by his tree are still there to play with, and he still naps in his hollow, but they aren't tasks any more. The people keep to looping routines, which tell you when each one is busy: the camper pegs out his tent, then sits roasting marshmallows by the fire with his back to his backpack, then goes to the table for pizza; the low-poly man dances, then fetches a drink from the cooler; the girl dances, then warms her hands at the fire. Next to something he can use, a chalk E shows; hold E for slow jobs, and a ring fills as he works. Jobs make noise, and the people hear it and come to look ("?" over their heads), but the music drowns a lot of it out, and while they dance they're lost in the music and see less. The tasks:
- **Steal the marshmallows:** while the camper roasts with his back to it, hold E at his backpack to unzip it; the bag tumbles out. Carry it home to his stash under his tree. Running with it, it crinkles.
- **Turn the music off:** hold E at the plug under the table to tug it out with his teeth. The music stops, which ticks it off, and the dancers stop dead for two seconds: get away then. Then everyone wonders where the music went, and the low-poly man finds the plug wherever he left it and plugs it back in. Without the music, every noise carries further.
- **Raid the cooler:** hold E to nose its lid open (a clunk the camper hears if he's by the fire), or wait for the low-poly man, who sometimes leaves it open after his drink. Take the sausages home.
- **Caught carrying their things,** a man snatches them back and the puzzle resets: the bag zipped back in, the sausages back in the shut cooler.

There's no ending yet. Pictures are in [design/level1/tasks/](design/level1/tasks/).

**The tutorial at the camp and the campers' cones** (26 Oct 2026, `scripts/camp_tutorial.gd`, `scripts/camp_person.gd`, `scripts/vision_cone.gd`): on the way there, the only task is to investigate the music. When he reaches the camp, the game pauses and a note at the bottom says to press Tab. THE PLAN opens with the camp's three tasks on it, under one main task, Rock the party, and the note says to sneak past them; Tab again, and the game carries on. Only then can the campers see him, and their cones show on the ground: pale yellow while they watch, shorter while he sneaks. The moment one spots him, that one's cone turns red for 2 seconds, and then all the cones go while they guard, chase and shoo as before. Once he's got away, they look about, confused, with "??" over their heads, then walk back; each one's cone comes back 5 seconds after they start back. The fades on the cones are still to come, with the cone shader for Assignment 5.

**The party next door** (25 Oct 2026, `scripts/sound_waves.gd`): under the title the night is quiet; New Game starts the party up. You don't hear it (his lullaby plays on); you see it, as its sound waves. They are drawn like the thought icons, three hand-scribbled wavy white lines. On the beat, while the speaker's off the screen, a set pulses on the edge of the screen the music's coming from, so you can always tell which way to go; once the speaker's on the screen, the sets come out of the speaker itself. Asleep in his hollow, he sleeps on through it, untroubled. Pictures are in [design/level1/waves/](design/level1/waves/).

**Controls:** WASD or the arrow keys to move, Shift to run, Ctrl or C to sneak, F to jump (tap it for a small hop, hold it for a full jump), E or a click to grab or drop, Space to chitter, and the mouse wheel to zoom. Walk into a tree to climb it. Then W and S climb up and down, A and D go round the trunk, and E or F lets go. Climb to the top of the home pine to get into the hollow. Esc pauses. M turns the music on and off, and N does the same for the sound effects. Tab brings up THE PLAN, the level's tasks on a torn notebook page, crossed off as they're done (the camp's tasks appear on it with the tutorial at the camp); the task to follow now waits at the bottom of the screen, and a task just done comes up there crossed off. V opens a panel for trying out camera views live; its "Copy numbers" button copies the settings.

**The automated sound check:** run `godot --headless --path . -- --sound-test`. It plays a scripted input sequence, counts how often each sound effect starts, and checks the music's pause, mute, loop and end behaviour. It prints a table, and its exit code is 0 only if every check passes (`scripts/sound_test.gd`).

**The campsite check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --camp-test`. It puts the raccoon near the camp sneaking, in plain sight, lingering, up a tree, gone and chittering out of sight, and checks how each of the three takes it (`scripts/camp_test.gd`). Add `--camp-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.

**The tasks check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --tasks-test`. It walks the three through their routines, then plays each task with E as you would: the marshmallows caught and snatched back, then stolen cleanly and taken home; the music off, the dancers frozen, and the plug found and put back; a noise drowned by the music but heard without it; and the cooler raided. It checks the to-do list ticks each one off (`scripts/tasks_test.gd`). Add `--tasks-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.

**The sound waves check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --waves-test`. It checks a set of waves goes out on the party's beat and fades after its time; that by his tree and along the trail they're on the edge of the screen the music comes from, and at the camp they come out of the speaker; and that with the music stopped no more come (`scripts/waves_test.gd`). Add `--waves-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.

**THE PLAN check:** run `godot --headless --path . --audio-driver Dummy -- --plan-test`. It brings the plan up with Tab and puts it away, checks V has the camera panel, then ticks tasks off and checks what comes up at the bottom of the screen: a task just done, crossed off, and gone again; the key task waiting there until he reaches the camp; and the page crossing off what's been done (`scripts/plan_test.gd`). Add `--plan-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures.

**The tutorial and cones check:** run `godot --headless --path . -- --cones-test`. It puts the raccoon in plain sight at the camp and checks that nobody sees him before the tutorial; that the tutorial pauses the game, ignores Esc, shows Rock the party and its tasks on Tab and carries on after a second Tab; that the spotter's cone is red, every cone shows through the red, and every cone goes 2.5 s after the spotting; that after the chase each of them is confused for 3 s and their cone comes back 5 s after they start back; and that Rock the party is ticked off with its last task (`scripts/cones_test.gd`). It measures the times on the game's clock, so it passes the same at `--fixed-fps 30`, `60` and `144`. Add `--cones-shots=<folder>` in a window for pictures. The other checks skip the tutorial.

**The title screen check:** run `godot --headless --path . -- --title-test`. It moves through the menu with the keys and the mouse, changes the volumes and checks they reach the buses and the settings file, checks the menu's keys leave him asleep, then chooses New Game and checks the way in: the same scene throughout with nothing laid over it, the camera ending in the nap close-up, the lullaby carrying on, the party next door quiet under the title and starting with New Game, silent, with the lullaby playing on and his nap going on untroubled by it, that first nap not counting as one of his naps, and a move key waking him and bringing in the forest music and the key task at the bottom of the screen. It puts your settings file back afterwards (`scripts/title_test.gd`). Run in a window with `--title-shots=<folder>` as well, it saves pictures of the way in. `godot --path . -- --title-shot=out.png` saves a picture of the title screen.

To redraw the storyboard after editing it, run `python design/storyboard/make_thumbnails.py`. To remake the character-sheet images and the raccoon's cut-outs, run `godot --path . --script res://design/character/make_character_sheet.gd`, then copy the five cut-outs the slice uses into `assets/characters/raccoon/`. For the stump, run `godot --headless --path . --script res://design/environment/make_props.gd`. For the sound loops, run `python design/sfx/make_sfx_loops.py`. To update the game's raccoon after editing `raccoon.blend`, run `blender -b assets/characters/raccoon.blend --python assets/characters/export_raccoon.py`.
